THOUGHT: This 5-year-old boy presents with asymptomatic systemic hypertension detected incidentally at a well-child visit. His blood pressure of 150/80 mm Hg in the right upper extremity is markedly elevated for age (≥95th percentile for systolic BP in a 5-year-old is ~114 mm Hg; 150 mm Hg is >99th percentile + 5 mm Hg, indicating stage 2 hypertension). The physical exam reveals a classic triad suggestive of coarctation of the aorta: (1) upper extremity hypertension, (2) weak or delayed femoral pulses (described as “trace” — i.e., diminished), and (3) a systolic ejection click and a 2/6 systolic murmur over the left sternal border and back — consistent with turbulent flow across a discrete aortic narrowing and possible associated bicuspid aortic valve (ejection click implies abnormal but mobile semilunar valve, commonly bicuspid in coarctation). The echocardiogram confirms the diagnosis: narrowing of the aorta distal to the left subclavian artery with a measurable gradient — the hallmark anatomic and hemodynamic finding of coarctation. The BP differential (upper > lower extremities) further supports this. Rib notching is absent on CXR, which is expected in young children, as it develops over years due to collateral vessel erosion of ribs. No other secondary causes (e.g., renal artery stenosis, endocrine disorders, chronic kidney disease) are suggested by history, exam, or testing; the presentation is typical for isolated, native coarctation — often undetected in early childhood if collateral circulation is sufficient to mask symptoms.

DIAGNOSIS: Coarctation of the aorta
